task: Process journal for Criterion B Developing: 'Place and Memory' unit. Show how you explored ideas, experimented with media and composition, and developed a clear artistic intention for your final piece.
text:
Process Journal - Criterion B: Developing
MYP Visual Arts Year 5
Name: Isla Fernandes

Slide 2 - Contents
1. My starting point
2. Exploring ideas: thumbnails and mind map
3. Experiments with media
4. Composition studies
5. Testing the colour scheme
6. Responding to feedback
7. Artistic intention and plan for the final piece

Slide 3 - Starting point
Unit: "Place and Memory". I have decided to make a large mixed media painting of the fish market in Colva, Goa, where my grandmother used to take me every Saturday.

What interests me is that the market is a place that I only really remember through the senses: the smell of salt and diesel, the noise, the wet floor shining under the strip lights. I do not want to paint a photograph of the market. I want to paint how it feels to remember a place that is changing, because the old market is being rebuilt with a concrete hall.

Slide 4 - Mind map
Centre: MARKET MEMORY
Branches: sound (haggling, radios), smell (can only be shown through colour and texture?), movement (crowds, women bending), light (strip lights vs. daylight), change (old tin roof / new concrete)
Annotation: I circled "light" and "change" because these two could be shown visually. Smell and sound are hard, so I will try to suggest them through mark-making instead of objects.

Slide 5 - Thumbnail sketches (6)
Thumbnail 1 - single seller, close up. Too much like a portrait, loses the sense of place.
Thumbnail 2 - wide view from above. Boring, everything the same size.
Thumbnail 3 - view from low down, through the legs of the crowd. Interesting, feels like a child's view which is what my memory actually is.
Thumbnail 4 - tin roof dividing the picture in half, old market above, concrete below.
Thumbnail 5 - fish only, abstract silver shapes.
Thumbnail 6 - combination of 3 and 4.
Decision: continue with 6, because it keeps the child's eye view and also says something about change.

Slide 6 - Influence from artists (short)
I looked at Nicolas de Stael for how he builds thick flat blocks of colour with a palette knife so that a landscape becomes almost abstract. I looked at Atul Dodiya for how he layers memory and everyday objects. I am borrowing the knife technique from de Stael, not his colours, because his greys would make my market feel cold.

Slide 7 - Experiment 1: watercolour wash
Photo of a small watercolour study of the roof and stalls.
Annotation: too watery, the colours bled together and the fish lost their shape. Good for the light on the wet floor though, so I will keep watercolour only as a thin first layer under the acrylic.

Slide 8 - Experiment 2: acrylic with palette knife
Photo of A5 study.
Annotation: thick paint makes the silver fish look solid and heavy like they really are. The knife leaves ridges which catch real light. Problem: I used too much white and the picture looks chalky.
Next: try mixing a little ultramarine into the whites to make them cooler and more like the fluorescent light.

Slide 9 - Experiment 3: acrylic plus collage
I glued torn pieces of newspaper (the Konkani paper my grandmother reads) under the paint on the floor area.
Annotation: it works because the print shows through in patches and gives the feeling of wet paper on a market floor. But it also gets distracting when the text is readable. I will only use pieces where the text is upside down or covered so it is texture and not information.

Slide 10 - Experiment 4: oil pastel resist
I drew the outlines of the baskets with oil pastel and then painted a watercolour wash over it.
Annotation: the wash slides off the pastel and leaves clean lines, which is good for the baskets. But it looks too neat and decorative, like a children's book, and not like a memory. I decided not to use this in the final.

Slide 11 - What I learned from the experiments
Watercolour: only as underlayer. Palette knife acrylic: yes, for fish and roof. Collage: yes, in the floor only, text hidden. Oil pastel resist: no.
So the final technique is a layered one: thin wash, collage, thick knife acrylic, and then scratching back with a sharpened brush handle for the lines of the crowd.

Slide 12 - Composition study 1
Rough grid study with rule of thirds lines drawn on top.
Annotation: roof line sits on the upper third which is good, but the cluster of people is exactly in the middle and it feels static. I want the eye to travel from the bright left side to the dark right.

Slide 13 - Composition study 2
I moved the people to the left third and added a diagonal made by the floor drains running from bottom right.
Annotation: much better. The diagonal pulls the eye in. Also I made the figures taller and cropped their heads off with the top edge, so the viewer is looking up like a child would. A teacher said this cropping felt unusual and brave, so I am keeping it.

Slide 14 - Colour scheme testing
Swatches:
A - warm (yellow ochre, vermilion) - too cheerful, like a tourist poster.
B - cold (ultramarine, grey, white) - matches the strip lights but is unfriendly.
C - mixed: warm sunlight orange coming through the tin roof against cold fluorescent blue-white on the floor.
I chose C because the clash between the two lights is actually what I remember, and it also supports my idea about old and new, with warm = old tin roof and cold = new concrete hall.

Slide 15 - Feedback
Peer feedback from Dev: "I can't tell what the shapes in the middle are."
Teacher feedback: the middle is a muddle and the figures all have the same posture.
My response: I made a new figure study in charcoal of three different poses (bending, carrying, pointing) and tested it in a small acrylic version. The new version has more variety and the middle is cleaner. Photo on slide 16.

Slide 16 - Small version of final (30 x 40 cm)
Annotation: this tells me the red of the crates is too strong and pulls the eye away from the fish. Will make the crates a duller brick colour in the final. Also the diagonal works.

Slide 17 - Time plan
Week 1: stretch and prime canvas, wash layer
Week 2: collage and drawing in
Week 3-4: knife acrylic
Week 5: scratching, final adjustments

Slide 18 - Artistic intention
My intention is to make a painting 100 x 120 cm that shows the Colva fish market as I remember it as a child: seen from low down, cropped, crowded and full of light, to communicate that memory is physical and a bit chaotic and that the place is being lost. I will use thin watercolour, hidden newspaper collage and thick palette knife acrylic. The warm orange of the old roof will fight with the cold blue-white of the new lights across the diagonal composition. I want the viewer to feel a bit small and surrounded, and also a bit sad, even if they do not know the market.

Slide 19 - Reflection on my development
At the start I thought experimenting was about finding the nicest looking result. Now I think it is about finding what answers my idea. Oil pastel resist looked "nicer" than many of my other tests but it said the wrong thing, so I dropped it. I also changed my thinking on composition: I used to just place things where they looked good, but with the diagonal I understood how composition can carry meaning. If I did it again I would test more textures for the tin roof, since I only tried one.

Slide 20 - Bibliography
Nicolas de Stael, Atul Dodiya (images from museum websites). Photographs of Colva market taken by me, 2023.

task: Submit your process journal showing your development of ideas for a self portrait on the theme of Identity, including experiments and your intention for the final artwork.
text:
Criterion B - Developing ideas
Process journal
Rohan Mehta, Art Year 5

Page 1 - Theme
The theme is "Identity". My idea is to make a self portrait that is not just my face but shows me as a person who plays cricket and also loves old Bollywood posters.

Page 2 - Initial ideas
Mind map with words: cricket bat, Dad's old radio, hand painted posters, mirror, school uniform, bright colours.
I did four thumbnail ideas.
1. Me holding the bat, plain background.
2. Me as a poster for a film called "The Last Over".
3. Half my face is photographic and half is painted.
4. My reflection in the cricket ball.
I chose number 2 because it is more fun and connects both of my interests. Number 1 looked boring and plain.

Page 3 - Looking at film posters
I looked at hand painted Bollywood posters from the 1970s. They use really bright colours, huge faces, and the title in bold lettering with a lot of drama. The faces are often very big with lots of rays of light coming from behind them. I want to use the sun ray idea behind my head.

Page 4 - Experiment: pencil sketches
Three sketches of my face from a photo.
Annotation: sketch 1 proportions wrong, eyes too high. Sketch 2 better after I used the guidelines (eyes halfway). Sketch 3 good, I will use this one.

Page 5 - Experiment: acrylic colour blocks
I tried painting the face in flat colours like a poster, using three skin tones (light, mid, shadow).
Annotation: this worked well because the flat colours look like a poster, but the shadows looked a bit muddy where I mixed brown and green. Next time use burnt sienna and purple instead.

Page 6 - Experiment: radiating lines
I made rays in yellow and orange behind the head with a ruler and with a brush.
Annotation: ruler lines were too perfect and looked like a computer made them. The brush ones are better because they are a bit wobbly like a hand-painted poster.

Page 7 - Experiment: lettering
I tried the title "THE LAST OVER" in three fonts by hand. The thick outlined one with a red shadow looks most like an old poster. Tried it in blue, was not good, red is better.

Page 8 - Composition
I drew the face large in the middle, the bat on the right diagonal, the title at the bottom and rays coming from behind the head. I tried it in two layouts, one with title at the top and one at the bottom. The bottom layout is better because the eyes are near the top third.

Page 9 - Colour
I decided on red, yellow, orange and a dark blue for the background so the rays pop. I tested the blue and it makes the yellow rays really bright.

Page 10 - Problems
At first the skin looked flat. I added a bit of highlight on the forehead and nose and it looks better. My teacher said the bat looks small so I made it larger in the second version.

Page 11 - Small version
A5 version made in acrylic. It shows all the ideas together. I think it works but the lettering is too close to the edge, so I need to leave a border.

Page 11b - Feedback from my group
Aarav said the face looked too serious for a funny poster. I tried a half smile on a tracing paper overlay and it looked better. Meera said the rays should reach the edge of the canvas. I tested this on the small version and agree, because it fills the space more.

Page 11c - Second small version
I made a second A5 version with the half smile, bigger bat, and the rays reaching the edges. I also added a small cricket ball in the corner. Annotation: ball is a bit random and does not add much, might remove. The border is now okay. This version is better than the first because the face is more friendly and the red lettering stands out more.

Page 11d - Materials list
Canvas 50 x 70, acrylic paint (red, yellow, orange, dark blue, white, burnt sienna), flat brushes size 10 and 4, a round brush for lettering, masking tape for the border, a ruler for the guidelines only.

Page 11e - Plan
Day 1 transfer drawing with a grid. Day 2 background blue and rays. Day 3 face in flat blocks. Day 4 lettering and bat. Day 5 final touches and fix mistakes.

Page 12 - Intention for final piece
I want to make a poster style self portrait on a 50 x 70 cm canvas which shows my identity as a cricketer and a fan of old films, using bright colours, flat blocks and big dramatic lettering so it is funny but also shows what is important to me.

Page 13 - Evaluation of development
I think my development went well. I changed the rays from ruler to brush and I added the bat bigger. I think I could have tried more ideas for the background and more ideas for the cricket part.

Page 14 - Extra note
I also practiced the lettering again on a spare page with the round brush because the first try had shaky edges. It is a bit better now. I will go slowly on the final.

task: Process journal for Criterion B Developing: show your exploration of ideas and techniques for a final piece on the theme of Nature and Structure.
text:
ART PROCESS JOURNAL
Criterion B Developing
Student: Tanvi

SLIDE 1: Title
"Nature and Structure" - Developing my ideas towards a final artwork
By Tanvi, Year 5 Visual Arts

SLIDE 2: Brief
The task was to create a final piece related to nature and structure. I chose leaves because I like leaves and they are everywhere in my garden. I also chose them because there are a lot of things you can do with leaves.

SLIDE 3: Mind map
Leaf - green - veins - autumn - pattern - tree - shape - garden - grow - seasons - light - shadows - water - insect holes - dry - wet
I looked at lots of things you can see in a leaf. I wrote them down in a spider diagram. Then I drew lines to see which ones went together.

SLIDE 4: Photographs
I took 12 photographs of leaves in my garden and on the way to school. [image of leaves]
The first photograph is a big leaf on the ground. The second photograph is a small leaf on a branch. The third photograph is some leaves together. The fourth photograph is a leaf with a hole. The fifth photograph is a yellow leaf. The sixth photograph is a leaf on a wall. The seventh photograph is leaves in water.

SLIDE 5: Sketches
I did 10 sketches of leaves in pencil. [image of 10 sketches]
Sketch 1 is of a banana leaf. Sketch 2 is of a mango leaf. Sketch 3 is of a hibiscus leaf. Sketch 4 is of a curry leaf. Sketch 5 is of a peepal leaf. They have different shapes. I used a 2B pencil for the sketches and I shaded some of them.

SLIDE 6: Artist research - Georgia O'Keeffe
Georgia O'Keeffe was born in 1887 in Wisconsin. She is known as the Mother of American modernism. She studied at the Art Institute of Chicago and the Art Students League in New York. She was married to Alfred Stieglitz, a photographer. She painted flowers, skulls, and New Mexico landscapes. She died in 1986 in Santa Fe aged 98. She painted big close up pictures of flowers such as Jimson Weed and Black Iris. [image of O'Keeffe painting]

SLIDE 7: Artist research - Ernst Haeckel
Ernst Haeckel was a German biologist and artist born in 1834. He made a book called Kunstformen der Natur which means Art Forms in Nature. It has 100 prints of animals and plants. His drawings are very detailed. He died in 1919. [image]

SLIDE 8: Experiment 1 - Pencil drawing of a leaf
I drew a large leaf in pencil. I drew the veins. It took 2 hours. I used a 4B pencil. [image]
It looks good.

SLIDE 9: Experiment 2 - Watercolour
I painted a leaf in watercolour. I used green and yellow. I painted the veins in dark green. [image]
It looks nice. The colours are nice.

SLIDE 10: Experiment 3 - Pen and ink
I used a black fine liner pen to draw leaf veins. I did lots of tiny lines. [image]
This took a long time. It looks quite good.

SLIDE 11: Experiment 4 - Acrylic
I painted a big leaf with acrylic paint. I used light green, dark green and yellow. [image]
It looks good but a bit messy.

SLIDE 12: Experiment 5 - Printmaking
I used a real leaf and green paint and pressed it on paper to make a print. I did this lots of times with different leaves. [image of leaf prints]
The prints are nice. Some came out better than others.

SLIDE 13: Experiment 6 - Collage
I cut up some green paper and stuck it down to make a leaf. [image]
It was a bit difficult but looks interesting.

SLIDE 14: Experiment 7 - Oil pastels
I used oil pastels to colour a leaf. I used green, yellow and orange. [image]
Oil pastels are quite smudgy. I do not like them as much.

SLIDE 15: Experiment 8 - Charcoal
I used charcoal to draw a big leaf. [image]
It looks dark. It was messy on my hands.

SLIDE 16: Experiment 9 - Digital
I used a drawing app on my iPad to draw leaves. I used different brushes. [image]
It was easy and I could undo things.

SLIDE 17: Experiment 10 - Mixed media
I used watercolour and then drew the veins with pen on top. [image]
This was my favourite one so far and it looks good.

SLIDE 18: More artist research - Karl Blossfeldt
Karl Blossfeldt was a German photographer who lived from 1865 to 1932. He took close up black and white pictures of plants. His book is called Urformen der Kunst. He was a teacher at the Berlin University of the Arts. [image]

SLIDE 19: Composition
I made three composition drawings. One has one leaf in the middle. One has lots of leaves. One has leaves in a circle. [image] I will choose the one with lots of leaves.

SLIDE 20: Colour
I will use green, yellow, orange and brown because those are colours leaves are.

SLIDE 21: Photo of leaf under magnifying glass
I used a magnifying glass to look at the veins. They look like a river map. I drew this. [image]

SLIDE 22: Another sketch
Sketch of a big banana leaf with a split. [image]

SLIDE 23: Another sketch
Sketch of a leaf with insect holes. [image]

SLIDE 24: Another sketch
Sketch of leaves on the ground. [image]

SLIDE 25: Another watercolour
Watercolour of autumn leaves in yellow, orange and red. [image]
Looks nice.

SLIDE 25b: Another pen drawing
Pen drawing of leaf veins on a hibiscus leaf. Took one hour. [image]

SLIDE 25c: Another print
Leaf print using orange paint. [image] I did four of these. The orange one looks nice. The green ones are better than the orange ones.

SLIDE 25d: Another collage
I tried collage again with brown and yellow paper. [image] This one was easier. I stuck them with glue stick.

SLIDE 25e: Colour wheel
I made a colour wheel to see which colours go with green. Green goes with yellow and blue. [image]

SLIDE 25f: Photographs 2
I took 8 more photographs of leaves. The first one is a leaf in the sun. The second one is a leaf in the shade. The third one is a leaf in the rain. The fourth is a leaf on the road. The fifth is a leaf on my desk. [image]

SLIDE 25g: Sketch of leaves from above
Another leaf sketch with pencil. [image] I like how it looks.

SLIDE 25h: Another experiment with acrylic
I painted a small leaf with acrylic again. [image] It is better than the first one.

SLIDE 25i: Teacher said
My teacher said I have done a lot of work. I need to choose one idea now.

SLIDE 25j: Reflection so far
I have done a lot of experiments. My favourite was watercolour and pen. I also liked printmaking. I did not like oil pastels or charcoal because they were messy. I think I am good at drawing leaves. I have done many different types of art with leaves and I have learned a lot about leaves and the different ways to draw them.

SLIDE 25k: Leaf facts
Leaves make food for the plant using sunlight. This is called photosynthesis. The green colour is from chlorophyll. In autumn the chlorophyll goes and leaves turn yellow, orange and red. Veins carry water and food. I put some of these facts in my sketchbook with a drawing. [image]

SLIDE 25l: Another pencil sketch
Sketch of a peepal leaf with a long tip. [image] It was hard to draw the tip.

SLIDE 25m: Another digital sketch
Leaf drawing in the app in dark green. [image] It looks quite good.

SLIDE 26: Final idea
My final piece will be a painting of many leaves. It will be in watercolour and pen. It will be A2 size. I will paint it in green, yellow, orange and brown.

SLIDE 27: Time plan
Week 1 pencil outline. Week 2 watercolour. Week 3 pen. Week 4 finish.

SLIDE 28: Bibliography
Wikipedia - Georgia O'Keeffe
Wikipedia - Ernst Haeckel
Wikipedia - Karl Blossfeldt
Google images

task: Investigate the Japanese ukiyo-e print tradition: explain its context and purpose, and write a critique of one artwork that shows how formal qualities carry meaning.
text:
Ukiyo-e and The Great Wave: how a print of the "floating world" speaks about danger and ordinary life

Ukiyo-e, meaning "pictures of the floating world", was the popular woodblock print art of Edo-period Japan, roughly 1603 to 1868. Its starting point is social. Under the Tokugawa shogunate a long peace had created a wealthy merchant class in Edo, who ranked low in the official hierarchy but had money to spend. They bought prints of kabuki actors, courtesans and, later, landscapes, because prints were cheap enough to be bought like posters or magazines. The "floating world" originally described the pleasure districts, with a Buddhist sense that life is fleeting, and so ukiyo-e often carries a mood of enjoying the moment while knowing it passes. This context matters because it explains why the art is bold and commercial instead of private and elite: a print had to catch the eye of a buyer within seconds.

The process also shaped the style. A print was a team product, made by the artist, a carver who cut the drawing into cherry wood, a printer, and a publisher who paid for it and sold it. Because every colour needed its own block, artists worked with flat areas of colour and strong outlines instead of soft shading. The introduction of Prussian blue in the 1820s, imported through Dutch traders, gave artists a strong colour that did not fade as quickly as the plant blues used before. Some of the thick, flat, graphic look that later impressed European artists such as Van Gogh and Monet comes directly from these technical limits, rather than from a wish to be "simple".

Katsushika Hokusai (1760-1849) made "Under the Wave off Kanagawa" around 1831 as part of the series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. By then travel and pilgrimage had become popular, and the series was sold to people who wanted pictures of famous places. What is unusual is that Hokusai does not give Fuji the dominant place that a buyer might expect. The mountain is small, and almost swallowed in the trough of the wave.

Looking at the print itself, the composition is built on a tension between two curves. The huge wave on the left curls over like a claw, its foam breaking into separate fingers, and the curve of its upper edge echoes the far smaller peak of Fuji, so that the mountain looks like a frozen version of the wave. Three fishing boats, with their rowers bending low, are pulled into the hollow. Their long low shape runs against the high curve of the wave, and the lines of the boats lead the eye towards the centre where the wave is about to fall. The palette is limited to Prussian blue, a pale sand colour and white. This restriction makes the print readable at a glance and makes the blue seem more intense, an effect that Hokusai would have valued because blue was the new and fashionable colour. The sky is a flat, yellowish grey, which pushes the wave forward and makes it appear almost solid.

The meaning is more complicated than "nature is powerful". The rowers are probably carrying fish to the Edo market, so these are working men, not heroes, and the print puts their daily danger beside the sacred permanence of Fuji. In my reading, this is where the print is most clever: the viewer is placed low, near the boat level, and so feels the wave from the point of view of those in danger, but the small calm mountain in the distance suggests that the wave will pass. It communicates the ukiyo-e idea of the fleeting world in a very concentrated way. Some writers also link the wave to the fear Japanese viewers might have had of foreign ships and change in the years before 1853, but I think this is less certain than the connection to everyday life, since the evidence for it is limited.

Its later reception shows why it is important. The print was produced in large numbers, so many copies survived, and it was collected in Europe after Japan opened to trade. Debussy reportedly asked for it on the cover of the score of La Mer. However, I should be careful because we know the Western fascination with Japan, called Japonisme, also exoticized the art and sometimes reduced it to a decorative wave. In Japan Hokusai was already a popular artist, not a lonely genius.

For my own work I will take three ideas from this study: use a limited palette to concentrate attention, let a small figure or element in the distance change the meaning of a large dramatic one, and place the viewer in the position of the person in danger, instead of watching from outside.

Sources: Britain, The British Museum, "Hokusai: Beyond the Great Wave" exhibition catalogue (2017); Metropolitan Museum of Art essay on Ukiyo-e; Timothy Clark, "The Great Wave" lecture notes; Calza, G., Hokusai (Phaidon).

task: Investigate an art movement (Pop Art) and write a critique of one artwork from it, explaining its context and how it communicates.
text:
Pop Art and Andy Warhol

Pop Art was an art movement that started in the 1950s in Britain and America. It used popular culture such as advertising, comics, celebrities and everyday products. The word "pop" comes from "popular". Some famous Pop artists are Andy Warhol, Roy Lichtenstein, Richard Hamilton, Claes Oldenburg and Jasper Johns. Pop Art was a reaction against Abstract Expressionism which was serious and emotional.

Andy Warhol was born on 6 August 1928 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. His real name was Andrew Warhola. His parents were immigrants from what is now Slovakia. His father worked in construction and died when Andy was 13. When Andy was a child he suffered from an illness called chorea, which made him stay in bed a lot. During this time he drew, listened to the radio and collected pictures of movie stars. His mother Julia encouraged him to draw. He studied pictorial design at the Carnegie Institute of Technology in Pittsburgh and graduated in 1949.

After graduating he moved to New York City and worked as a commercial illustrator. He made drawings for magazines such as Vogue and Harper's Bazaar and advertisements for shoe companies like I. Miller. He won awards for his illustrations. In the early 1960s he started to make paintings of Campbell's soup cans and Coca Cola bottles. His first exhibition of Campbell's Soup Cans was at the Ferus Gallery in Los Angeles in 1962. He painted 32 canvases, one for each flavour of soup that Campbell's sold at that time.

In 1963 he set up a studio called The Factory in New York. It was painted silver. Many artists, musicians, actors and other famous people visited it. He made silkscreen prints there using assistants. He made portraits of Marilyn Monroe after she died in 1962, Elizabeth Taylor, Elvis Presley, Mao Zedong and Jackie Kennedy. He also made films such as Chelsea Girls and Empire. He managed the band The Velvet Underground.

On 3 June 1968 he was shot by Valerie Solanas, a woman who had acted in one of his films. He nearly died but he survived. After this he had to wear a surgical corset for the rest of his life. In the 1970s and 1980s he continued to make portraits of rich and famous people on commission. He also started Interview magazine in 1969. He worked with the young artist Jean-Michel Basquiat in the 1980s. He died on 22 February 1987 in New York after a gallbladder operation, aged 58.

Campbell's Soup Cans (1962)
The artwork I chose to look at is Campbell's Soup Cans. It is made of 32 canvases which each measure 20 by 16 inches. Each canvas has a picture of a can of Campbell's soup. The cans are red and white with a gold circle and the name of the soup written in black letters, for example Tomato, Chicken Noodle, Cream of Mushroom and Pepper Pot. The background is white. The cans are painted in the middle of each canvas and they are all the same size. They are lined up in rows on a shelf like in a supermarket. The paint is acrylic on canvas. At first Warhol painted them by hand using a projector to trace the shape, and later he started to use a silkscreen method.

I think this artwork is effective because it is simple and it uses repeated images. The colours are bright and the cans look like real cans. The repeated pattern makes it look like a factory. It also looks like what you see in a supermarket. It is very recognisable and everybody knows what soup is. Some people think it is boring but I think it is interesting because it is different from what other artists painted.

Warhol said that he ate Campbell's soup for lunch every day for twenty years. When he was asked why he painted soup cans, he said it was because he was a commercial artist and he wanted to paint things that were familiar. When the paintings were shown in Los Angeles a gallery nearby put real cans in their window with a sign saying that they were cheaper. In 1996 the Museum of Modern Art in New York bought the set.

Other facts about Warhol
Warhol was very interested in fame. He is quoted as saying that in the future everyone will be world famous for 15 minutes. He had a collection of wigs, silver and white, and he was known for his shy manner and for speaking very little in interviews. He was a devout Byzantine Catholic and went to church often, and he secretly helped to feed homeless people at a church in New York. He had a pet dachshund called Archie. After he died, his will created the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, which gives money to artists. The Andy Warhol Museum in Pittsburgh opened in 1994 and it is the largest museum in America about one artist.

Conclusion
Pop Art is an important movement because it changed what art could be about. Andy Warhol was one of the most famous artists of the 20th century and his work is still famous today. Campbell's Soup Cans is one of the best known artworks in the world. It shows the movement's interest in popular culture.

Bibliography: Wikipedia, "Andy Warhol"; The Andy Warhol Museum website; Tate website; Britannica.

task: Investigate an art movement and write about one artwork from it.
text:
Impressionism

Impressionism was an art movement from France in the 1800s. It started in the 1860s and 1870s. The artists painted outside and used quick brush strokes and bright colours. They painted light. The name came from a painting called Impression, Sunrise by Claude Monet.

Famous Impressionists are Monet, Renoir, Degas, Pissarro and Cezanne. Monet was born in 1840 and died in 1926. He painted water lilies in his garden at Giverny. He painted lots of paintings of the same thing at different times of day, like haystacks and Rouen Cathedral.

I chose to look at Water Lilies by Monet. It is a painting of a pond with water lilies on it. The colours are blue, green, pink and purple. The brush strokes are small and soft. It looks like water and it is very beautiful. There is no horizon so you can't see where the water ends. I like this painting because it is relaxing and the colours are nice. Monet is one of my favourite artists.

Monet had his first big success with his paintings of the Seine. He lived in Argenteuil and later bought a house in Giverny in 1883. He had a Japanese bridge built over the pond. He had problems with his eyes because of cataracts in his old age and the colours in his later paintings became more red and yellow. He painted about 250 water lily paintings. Some are in the Musee de l'Orangerie in Paris, in two oval rooms.

Impressionism was important because it changed art and led to other movements.

task: Write an evaluation of your own final artwork and of your development as an artist during the unit, referring to your artistic intention.
text:
Evaluation of my final artwork, "Saturday, Colva" (acrylic, collage and watercolour on canvas, 100 x 120 cm)

My intention was to show the Colva fish market as I remember it from my childhood, seen from a child's low point of view, crowded and full of light, to communicate that memory is physical and chaotic and that this place is being lost to a concrete rebuild. Looking at the finished painting, I think I achieved most of this, but not all of it equally, and in some places the result is different from what I planned.

The strongest part is the composition. The diagonal I developed from the floor drains runs from the bottom right into the cluster of figures on the left third, and when I stand back from the canvas it pulls the eye through the picture exactly as I wanted. Cropping the heads of the standing figures with the top edge was a risk, because several people in my class said it looked unfinished in the small study. In the large painting it works well: the viewer is forced to look up at torsos, aprons and carrying baskets and so shares the height of a child. A visitor who knew nothing of my idea described the painting as "like being squeezed in a crowd", and that is the feeling I was after, so I consider this a success for my intention.

The colour scheme also does what it should in the top half. The warm orange light under the tin roof is painted in thick knife strokes of cadmium orange with a little yellow ochre pushed in, and against it the blue-white of the floor reads as cold. The clash is most effective at the point where the two meet, at the roof line on the upper third, because the edges are rough and the paint is thick enough to make a physical ridge. However, I think the colour contrast is weaker in the lower right, where I let the blue-white become too grey. I mixed in too much raw umber when I corrected a mistake on the drain, and the grey made that corner feel dull and flat compared with the rest. This is a weakness, because the lower right is where the diagonal starts and so should be strongest.

The technical handling is mixed. The palette knife works best on the fish, where the silver bodies are built in single sweeps and the thick paint makes them look heavy and wet. I am pleased that I mixed ultramarine into the whites, which was a decision from my second experiment, because the fish no longer look chalky. The collage under the floor was more risky. I hid the Konkani newsprint, as I had decided, so that it reads as texture, and I think it adds a feeling of wet paper. Yet I see now that in two patches the newsprint is still readable, and this draws the eye away from the figures. If I did the painting again I would paint over those with a thin glaze.

The idea of change, between the old tin roof and the new concrete hall, is the part that I think is least successful. In the plan I imagined warm for old and cold for new would be understood, but there is nothing in the painting that tells a viewer that a rebuild is happening. A viewer could think the warm and cold are simply two kinds of light. I could have added a small element, such as a piece of scaffolding or a concrete column in the far corner, and I considered this in my composition study but dropped it to keep the picture clean. Now I think I was wrong. That is the clearest gap between my intention and the result.

In terms of my development as an artist, I have learned that experiments are only valuable when they answer the idea. The oil pastel resist was the most attractive test and I rejected it because it was decorative, and this decision shaped how serious the final painting feels. I also learned to look at composition as meaning, not decoration. My earlier work was usually centred and safe. Here I took a risk with the crop and the diagonal, and receiving critique from my teacher and classmates made me change the figures' poses, which improved the middle of the painting a lot.

My next step as an artist is to work on mixing neutrals without letting them go dead, and to be braver about adding symbolic details that carry my idea. I would also like to test the same subject at a bigger scale with a knife only, because the knife marks were the most expressive part. Overall I judge the painting to be successful in atmosphere and viewpoint and partly successful in communicating change, and I know exactly what I would alter to improve it.

task: Evaluate your final self portrait: say how well it meets your intention and reflect on your growth as an artist.
text:
Evaluation of my final piece: "Last Over" self portrait

For my final piece I painted a poster style self portrait on a 50 x 70 cm canvas. My intention was to show my identity as a cricketer and as a fan of old Bollywood films, in bright colours with big dramatic lettering, so that it would be funny but also show what matters to me.

I think the piece is quite successful overall. The strongest part is the colour. The yellow and orange rays against the dark blue background are very bright and they make my face stand out in the centre. I tested the blue in my process and it was right to choose it, because a lighter blue would not have made the yellow glow. The rays are done by brush and not by ruler, which was a decision from my experiments, and I think the slight wobble helps it look hand painted like the real posters. The red lettering with the shadow is also good and it is the thing people noticed first when they looked at it in the class exhibition. The title "The Last Over" makes people smile, so it achieves the funny tone I wanted.

The weaker part is the face. I painted it in flat blocks of three skin tones, but in the final painting the blending between the mid tone and the shadow on the left cheek is uneven and in one area it is muddy, which is the problem I had in my first experiment too. I did not fully solve it, even though I decided to use burnt sienna and purple. I think I rushed this on day three. The half smile is better than the serious face of my first version, but the mouth is slightly crooked.

The bat is bigger as my teacher advised, and the diagonal helps the composition. However, the cricket ball that I said I might remove is still in the corner and it does not add much. It makes the corner a bit crowded and I would take it out if I did it again.

In terms of my own development I think I have improved at planning. At the start of this unit I just painted and hoped, and this time I made small versions and changed things like the border and the lettering position before the final. I also learned that looking at real hand painted posters helped me more than just thinking of my own ideas. Next time I want to practise skin tones and blending more, and to try a more complicated background than a single colour. I would like to try painting my portrait in a different style, such as realistic, to see if I can show a different side of my identity.

One more thing I learned is that I should photograph my work in good light before I give it in, because the photo I took makes the colours look duller than they are in real life.

To sum up, my final piece does show my identity and is bold and funny, and the colours work well, but the face painting has some problems and some details are unnecessary.

task: Evaluate your final artwork and say how you have developed as an artist.
text:
Evaluation

My final piece is a drawing of a dog on A3 paper with pencil. I think it came out good. I like the fur because it looks like real fur and I spent a lot of time on it. The ears are better than the sketch. I did not like the tail because it is a bit small. My friends said it looks like a real dog and I am happy with it.

I think my work is quite good and I worked hard. I learned that pencil is good for drawing animals. Next time I will try to draw a bigger one. I would like to do a cat.

I also think the paper I used was good because it was thick. I used a rubber a lot and it did not tear. My teacher said I should draw every day. The background is white and I think it looks clean. I am going to put it on my wall at home.

task: Submit your complete MYP Visual Arts coursework (process journal, investigation, artwork and evaluation) for assessment against criteria A, B, C and D.
text:
Process Journal: "Rising Water"
Year 5 Visual Arts
Name: Aditya Nair

Slide 2 - Idea in one sentence
A three panel linocut and acrylic piece about how my street in Chembur floods every monsoon and how my family carries on as normal.

Slide 3 - Where the idea came from
Last July the water in our lane reached the second step of our building. I took photos from the balcony. What surprised me was not the water but the calm: neighbours carrying school bags on their heads, a boy in a plastic bag poncho on a cycle, my aunt laughing while she held a bucket. I want to show that mix of disaster and routine.

Slide 4 - Mind map
FLOOD: brown water, reflections, umbrellas, rubbish, rickshaws stuck, stairs, light from shops at 6pm, people looking down, feet, rope.
Highlighted: reflections, feet, stairs.

Slide 5 - Thumbnails (8)
1. Street view from balcony. Too flat.
2. Feet in water, no faces. Strong. People shown only by legs and reflections.
3. Rickshaw stuck, close up. Funny but it is about the rickshaw not the people.
4. Stair steps going into water. Simple. Could be centre panel.
5. Umbrella from above, a circle in water.
6. Reflection of shop lights, abstract.
7. Boy on cycle, side view.
8. Triptych layout: left stairs, middle feet, right shop lights.
Decision: Use 8. It gives a sequence: water arrives (stairs), life goes on (feet), the evening (lights).

Slide 6 - Why triptych
I tested the format by making three small paper rectangles and arranging them. If the middle panel is wider than the other two, the eye settles there. Middle = 40 cm, sides = 25 cm each. Total width 90 cm, height 60 cm.

Slide 7 - Experiment 1: linocut test
Cut a small block of the stair steps in 10 x 10 cm lino.
Annotation: the lino cut easily but my lines are chunky. Black ink on white paper looks harsh. Good for hard edges of the steps, not for water.

Slide 8 - Experiment 2: linocut in blue-grey ink
Same block printed in blue-grey on brown kraft paper.
Annotation: the brown paper gives the feeling of muddy water. Much better than white. Keep kraft paper.

Slide 9 - Experiment 3: reduction print attempt
I tried to print the feet in two colours by cutting more after the first print.
Annotation: I misregistered the second layer by 3 mm and it looks messy. Maybe the blurriness suggests ripples in the water, so not a total failure. But for the main panels I will use separate blocks and register with pins.

Slide 10 - Experiment 4: acrylic washes over prints
Painted diluted burnt sienna over the blue-grey print.
Annotation: the ink does not resist the paint as I thought, it smudged. Next time seal with a thin layer of matte medium. Tested this on a second print and it worked.

Slide 11 - Experiment 5: showing reflections
How to show the reflection of feet in water? Tried (a) printing the block upside down below the original, (b) painting the reflection with thin wet paint and wiping it with a rag, (c) scratching lines into a painted surface.
Annotation: (a) too neat and mirror-like. (b) soft and realistic but I lost the lino texture. (c) most interesting because the scratches look like ripples. Combined plan: print the feet, then paint a thin brown-green reflection under them and scratch ripple lines.

Slide 12 - Experiment 6: texture for the water
Tried sponge, a toothbrush, and a comb dragged through wet acrylic.
Annotation: the comb gives parallel lines like moving water. Sponge gives a grainy dirty feel which is also good for flood water. I will use comb for the centre and sponge for the edges.

Slide 13 - Colour tests
Palette A: brown, grey-green, yellow lights. Palette B: add red from a rickshaw. Palette C: only brown and blue-grey with a spot of yellow.
I picked C. The yellow spot of shop light looks stronger when everything else is muted, and it shows the warmth of people inside. Red was too loud and made it look like a poster about danger.

Slide 14 - Composition studies for the middle panel
Version 1: feet in a row across the middle. Looked like a frieze, boring.
Version 2: feet at different heights, some stepping up the stairs. Better rhythm.
Version 3: added a child's feet in small yellow boots. This one has a focal point and a story. Chosen.

Slide 15 - Feedback session
Peer (Sana): the left panel has no clear centre. Teacher: the stairs should be seen from a lower angle so that the water feels like it is rising towards the viewer.
My response: redrew the stairs from low down, with steps getting bigger toward the front. See slide 16.

Slide 16 - Revised left panel sketch
Annotation: the low angle makes the steps look like a cliff, which is dramatic but also a bit funny since it is only a few steps. I think it is good because it shows how big a few steps feel when water is coming.

Slide 17 - Test of the full triptych at small scale
Made a 30 x 20 cm version with all three panels.
Annotation: the left and middle panels connect well because the water line is at the same height across both. The right panel with the shop lights is too different, so I added a line of silhouettes of legs from the middle panel at the bottom of the right panel.

Slide 18 - Problems and solutions
Problem: ink smudged under paint. Solution: matte medium seal.
Problem: lino blocks warp slightly. Solution: warm them before printing.
Problem: reflections too dark. Solution: use more water in the wash and wipe.
Problem: yellow boots disappear. Solution: outline with a thin dark line.

Slide 19 - Artistic intention
I intend to make a triptych 90 x 60 cm in linocut and acrylic on kraft paper that shows a flooded Mumbai street as a place where people continue with everyday life. By using a low viewpoint, a muted brown and blue-grey palette, and one warm yellow light, I want the viewer to feel both the threat of the water and the quiet strength of the people, so the mood is calm and slightly humorous instead of tragic.

Slide 20 - Plan
Week 1: carve three blocks. Week 2: print on kraft paper, edition of 3 to choose best. Week 3: seal, paint the reflections and scratch. Week 4: add yellow light and boots; mount on board.

Slide 21 - Techniques I will use
Relief printing with oil-based ink, brayer, pin registration, matte medium seal, acrylic wash, sgraffito with a comb and a scraper, sponge texture.

Slide 22 - Time log
Mon: thumbnail sketches 1 hr. Wed: lino tests 2 hr. Fri: colour tests 1 hr. Mon: composition studies 1.5 hr. Wed: feedback and redraw 1 hr. Fri: small version 2 hr.

Slide 23 - Materials and safety
V-gouge, U-gouge, bench hook so I do not cut my hand, oil-based ink, brayer, kraft paper, acrylic paints (burnt sienna, ultramarine, raw umber, cadmium yellow), matte medium, comb, sponge.

Slide 24 - Note on reflection
Overall I can see how my ideas moved from a simple photo of the street to a plan where each panel has a job: water arrives, life goes on, evening lights. I am now more confident that I can plan a long work before starting it. I would still like to test one more material for the water, perhaps clear gel, in case the comb texture looks too regular in the final.

Slide 24b - Experiment 7: scale of the stairs panel
I printed the stairs block at two sizes, 10 x 10 and 25 x 25 cm. At the bigger size the carving lines look rougher and more like rough concrete, which suits the subject. At the small size the edges looked fussy. Decision: carve the final block directly at full size, using a larger gouge for the steps and the V-gouge only for the water lines.

Slide 24c - Experiment 8: inking
Too much ink fills the fine cuts and the print looks blotchy. Too little gives a speckled look. I tested three amounts. The middle amount gave a slightly uneven edge, a bit like a wet surface. I decided to roll the brayer twice in two directions and print with a wooden spoon, not a press, to keep the uneven look.

Slide 24d - Experiment 9: yellow light
Tried the yellow in three ways: cadmium yellow straight, mixed with a little white, and glazed thinly over the burnt sienna. The glazed one glows and looks like light through murky water. Chosen. Annotation: it must be applied last or the ink under it picks up.

Slide 24e - Experiment 10: edge of the panels
Tested torn paper edges and cut edges. Torn edges look softer, a bit like paper that has been wet. I will tear the kraft paper against a ruler and mount the three panels with a 2 cm gap so the water line continues across but the panels still read as separate.

Slide 25 - Photographs of my progress
[image: lino blocks] [image: test prints] [image: palette] [image: small version]

Slide 26 - Reference photos
My own photos of Chembur street, July. No other sources.

task: Write an evaluation of your final artwork and your development as an artist.
text:
Evaluation of my final artwork - "Garden Pond"

My final artwork is a painting of a garden pond. It is done in acrylic paint on a canvas that is 40 cm by 50 cm. I am going to evaluate it by describing what I did, step by step, and then say what I think.

First, I started with the background. I painted the whole canvas with a light blue colour. I used a big flat brush for this and I painted from the top to the bottom. Then I waited for it to dry for about twenty minutes. After this I painted the sky in the top part of the canvas. The sky is light blue and white. I made the white clouds by dabbing the white paint on with the brush. There are three clouds. One cloud is on the left, one is in the middle and one is on the right.

Next, I painted the trees. The trees are on the left side of the painting and on the right side of the painting. I used dark green for the leaves and brown for the trunks. The trunk of the left tree is thicker than the trunk of the right tree. I painted the leaves by making small dots with the end of a medium brush. I used a lighter green on top of the dark green so the leaves would look like they had sun on them. I used yellow and green mixed together to make the light green colour.

After the trees, I painted the pond in the middle of the canvas. The pond is an oval shape. I painted it in dark blue and then I added some green and some white to make the water look like water. In the pond there are three lily pads. They are round and green. I painted a pink flower on top of the biggest lily pad. The flower has five petals and a yellow centre. I used pink and white to make the petals. After that I painted two orange fish in the water, which are swimming to the left. I drew them with a thin brush and added black dots for the eyes.

Then I painted the grass around the pond. The grass is green and I used the thin brush to make lots of lines going up. There is long grass and short grass. I used three different greens for the grass: dark green, medium green and yellow-green. I also painted some rocks at the edge of the pond. The rocks are grey and I put some white on top and some black underneath. There are five rocks on the right side of the pond and three on the left.

Finally I painted a small bridge over the pond. The bridge is brown and has a curved shape. I painted the wood lines with a thin black brush. I put a small red flower next to the bridge and a yellow flower on the other side. I signed my name in the bottom right corner using black paint.

The colours in my painting are blue, green, brown, pink, orange, yellow, red, grey, white and black. The shapes in my painting are ovals for the pond, circles for the lily pads and a curve for the bridge. The painting is quite colourful.

When I look at my painting now I think it looks good. I think the painting is quite nice and the colours are nice. I think I did well on the trees and the pond. The fish look quite good and the flowers look pretty. I am quite happy with my painting.

I had some problems when I was painting. The grass was hard to do and the rocks took a long time. The paint dried too fast so I had to mix new colours a few times. I fixed it by adding more paint.

In the lessons I learned how to use acrylic paint. I made some mistakes but I fixed them. I learned about mixing colours to make light green and dark blue. My painting took five lessons to finish.

To conclude, I painted a pond with trees, a bridge, fish, flowers and rocks. It is a colourful painting and I think it is good. I would like to paint more things in the future.

task: Process portfolio and comparative study: investigate how two artists from different contexts deal with loss of place, and show how this informs the development of your own ideas and technical skills.
text:
Process Portfolio and Comparative Study: Where do bodies go when a place is taken away?

Contextual focus
My enquiry began with a question about my own city, Delhi, where the settlement my grandmother's family lived in until 2015 was cleared for a flyover. I want to look at how artists make the loss of home visible without turning people into victims. I compared two works made in different cultures and decades: Doris Salcedo's "Shibboleth" (2007, Tate Modern Turbine Hall) and Sheba Chhachhi's "Seven Lives and a Dream" (2012, India), alongside a close study of Kader Attia's "Repair" series for method.

Comparison of Salcedo and Chhachhi
Salcedo's work is a 167 metre crack that runs across the concrete floor of the Turbine Hall. She has described it as a way of showing the gap between those who have rights in Europe and the migrants who are excluded, and the title refers to a biblical word used to identify and exclude outsiders. What I find most useful in her practice is that she does not represent a person at all. The crack is a void and a threat, and visitors must walk along it, look into it and sometimes stumble on it. The context of the Tate, a building that was once a power station and is now a place of cultural capital, gives the crack a bitter irony, because the floor of an institution is literally split. She worked with engineers for months and used a metal mesh in the fissure, so the process itself was a kind of construction project that matches the idea of a hidden infrastructure of exclusion.

Chhachhi's work is built differently. "Seven Lives and a Dream" is a set of light boxes and installations that depict women whom she knew and interviewed, with layers of translucent photographs, text, and light. Where Salcedo withdraws the human figure, Chhachhi insists on it, gives people names and puts their stories in the foreground. The Indian context of the women's movement of the 1980s lies behind this practice, and her photographs come from long relationships rather than a single event. Looking at the two together, I noticed that they respond to the same problem in opposite ways: absence as a way to make the viewer feel loss, or presence as a way to resist erasure. Both use light and the space of the viewer, and both challenge a neutral gallery. I think Salcedo's piece risks becoming too abstract for someone who cannot read the context, whereas Chhachhi's risks becoming documentary, but I believe that the combination of the two helps me to decide what I want.

How this influenced my practice
I decided not to depict my grandmother's family in the way a journalist would. After looking at Salcedo, I tried to make the absence of the house the subject. After looking at Chhachhi, I realised I wanted names and objects, so I made my work a middle way: casting and projection of ordinary objects that were left behind.

Process portfolio (selected entries)
Entry 1, 3 March: I took clay and made impressions of the floor plan from my grandmother's drawing of the room, 3 x 4 metres, scaled down to 30 x 40 cm. The clay cracked as it dried. I first saw this as failure, but the crack ran through the doorway, and looking back at Salcedo I understood that the accident was meaningful. I decided to keep it and to control it by drying the next slab in the sun.

Entry 2, 14 March: I cast three objects in plaster: a steel tumbler, a door latch and a child's slipper. The slipper was a mistake because the plaster stuck to the rubber and broke when I removed it. I switched to alginate for the slipper mould and this gave a much finer surface. The latch worked best because the object is small and has a very specific shape; people recognise a latch even in white plaster. I realised that the cast objects look like fossils, which is relevant to the idea of a place being archaeologised even though it was only cleared a few years ago.

Entry 3, 29 March: I tested projection. I projected a short video of my grandmother's hands folding clothes onto the plaster floor plan. The hands moved across the cracks. It was too sentimental at first, with soft music, so I removed the sound, and the quiet made the cracks more important. A classmate said the hands looked like they were searching, and I had not intended this, but I decided to keep the idea of searching and slowed the video.

Entry 4, 10 April: Tried scale. Made a 2 x 3 metre version of the floor plan on the studio floor with cement dust and chalk and put the cast objects on it. The scale changed how people moved: viewers walked around it as if it were a real room and some stepped over the walls. This tells me that a full scale might make the work an environment and not a model. However, I did not have the space or enough material, so I decided on 1 x 1.5 metres as the final, large enough to walk around but not to enter.

Technical development
My control of casting improved from entry 2 to entry 4. I learned to oil the moulds and to vent the plaster, and I reduced air bubbles by tapping. With the clay I learned to slow the drying under damp cloths. With the projector I learned to keep the light low, so the plaster looked grey instead of white and the objects had shadows.

Where I am now
My final plan is an installation with a clay floor plan with its crack, three cast objects set at the positions where the doorway, the kitchen and the bed would have been, and the slow projection of hands. The viewer will have to walk along the crack. From Salcedo I take the use of the space of the viewer and the idea that a rupture can be a form, from Chhachhi I take the insistence on the particular, and from Attia I take the idea that a break can be repaired visibly with a different material. I will repair the crack with copper wire, not hide it. I still need to test whether the projection can be done on cement instead of plaster, and whether the copper reads as repair or decoration. I will do both tests next week.

Sources: Tate Modern, Unilever Series: Doris Salcedo, Shibboleth (2007), Tate Publishing; Chhachhi, S., "Seven Lives and a Dream" exhibition notes, Delhi; Kader Attia, "Repair: 5 Acts", Kunsthalle Bern interview; my grandmother's drawings and interview, recorded with permission, February.

task: Process portfolio: investigate artists connected to your theme of urban landscapes and show how you developed your ideas and skills through experiments.
text:
Visual Arts process portfolio - Investigation and development

Theme: Urban landscapes

For my project I looked at urban landscapes in my city, Pune. I wanted to make a series of paintings that show the city in an interesting way. I looked at the artist Edward Hopper and the artist David Hockney and I also took photos of different places in Pune.

Artist investigation
Edward Hopper was an American artist who lived from 1882 until 1967. He is famous for realist paintings of American life. His painting Nighthawks from 1942 shows people in a diner late at night. The painting has strong light and dark and the people look lonely. The diner is lit with a green-yellow light and the street outside is dark. I think Hopper uses light to create a lonely mood. He was influenced by the city of New York where he lived for most of his life. He painted a lot of empty rooms and streets. This is relevant to my work because I also want to show how a city can feel empty even though there are lots of people.

David Hockney was born in 1937 in Bradford, England. He is known for the pool paintings and for the bright colours he uses. A Bigger Splash from 1967 shows a swimming pool with a splash and a diving board. The colours are flat and bright and the composition is very simple. Hockney moved to California and the sunny light there is in his work. Later he also used iPads to draw. I like how the colours of Hockney are bright and I want to try them in my city pictures. His work is different to Hopper because it is happy and it is bright whereas Hopper is dark and quiet.

Comparing both artists, I find that they both paint modern life but in different ways. Hopper makes the viewer feel lonely while Hockney makes the viewer feel relaxed. Both of them use strong geometric shapes and flat areas of colour.

My photographs
I took photographs at Shaniwar Wada, FC Road, the railway station and Koregaon Park. I chose five of them to draw from. The first photo is of a street with lots of rickshaws. The second is a view of a bridge. The third is a view of tall buildings at sunset. The fourth is a crowded market. The fifth is of an empty bus stop at night.

Experiments
Experiment 1: I drew the rickshaw street in pencil and then I coloured it with colour pencils. The result was nice but I think the colours looked a bit flat. I also found it was hard to show the crowd.

Experiment 2: I painted the bus stop at night in acrylic using dark blue and yellow, which was inspired by Hopper. I think the light of the bus stop looks like the light in Nighthawks. I think this one works well and the mood is lonely. The yellow light looks good against the blue. A problem was that the road was too dark so you cannot see it.

Experiment 3: I painted the tall buildings in bright colours like Hockney. I used pink, orange and turquoise. It looks cheerful but a bit childish, and it does not look like Pune any more. I think the colours were too much.

Experiment 4: I tried a collage with magazine paper for the market. It was a bit messy. It was interesting to see that the bits of colour look like the crowds. I might use this idea again.

Choosing my direction
After the experiments I decided to continue with the dark night mood, because it worked better than the bright colours. I think this style fits my ideas about the city feeling empty. I will use acrylic paint on canvas. My final series will be three paintings of night scenes in Pune: the bus stop, the bridge, and an empty street with a single rickshaw.

Next steps
I need to improve my painting of the road. I will use a lighter blue-grey so it can be seen. I will also try a bigger canvas. I think my skills in painting have improved because I can now mix darker colours without making them muddy, but I need more practice with perspective. I will also try out some different brushes.

Sources: Wikipedia; Tate; Art Institute of Chicago website; my own photos.

task: Write a reflection and evaluation of your exhibition: how it communicated your intentions, how it was received, and how your practice has developed.
text:
Reflection and evaluation of my exhibition: "Threshold"

My exhibition "Threshold" consisted of six works: three large plaster and clay floor pieces about my grandmother's cleared home in Delhi, a projection of her hands, and two small cast works shown in a case. It was installed in the school gallery for ten days in March. I intend to reflect here on how successfully it communicated its ideas, how it was received, and how my practice has changed.

My aim was to make the viewer feel a loss that could not be seen: a place removed, a family dispersed. I wanted the work to be quiet, to avoid sentiment, and to make the viewer walk on and around the traces instead of looking at them from outside. To judge whether I had done this, I used three sources: my own observation of how people moved in the space, a feedback board where visitors wrote on cards, and a conversation with my teacher and a visiting artist.

The clearest success was the floor piece. I placed the clay floor plan at the centre so visitors could not avoid the crack that runs through the doorway. Over the ten days I noticed that nearly every viewer did one of two things: they walked around the plan as if respecting the walls, or they stepped over it and then looked guilty. Several said on their cards that they "didn't know if they were allowed". This reaction is precisely what I was hoping for, because it makes the viewer feel the trespass that clearance represents. I think it demonstrates that making the work physically accessible rather than behind a barrier was the right decision, and in the process portfolio I recorded that the scale test had suggested this. It also worked partly because I resisted my first impulse, which was to add a wall text with the history. The text I finally used was only a date and a location.

The projection was less successful. The slow video of my grandmother's hands, projected onto the plaster, drew many comments, but the comments suggest viewers read it as a nostalgic image of "an old woman" and did not link it to displacement. One visitor wrote "beautiful and sad", which is true but general. The problem, I think, was lighting: the gallery was too bright at the opening, so the projection became faint and the cracks across it could not be seen. After day two I covered the windows and the viewers' comments became more specific, with several mentioning "searching". It was a technical error on my part, because I should have tested the room at the same time of day as the opening. The adjustment showed me that I need to treat the exhibition space as a material and not only as a container.

The copper repair of the crack received very different responses. My teacher thought it was the most important decision in the show because it shows a repair that does not pretend the break never happened. A visiting sculptor, however, argued that it was too neat and made the crack look "designed" and so gave the story a consoling ending that my own research on Salcedo had warned about. I find this criticism fair. I had been influenced by Attia's idea of repair, but his repairs are visible and awkward. Mine were precise because I enjoy craft, and in this case craft may have worked against the meaning. In a future version I would make the stitches uneven, using thicker wire and a less careful hand.

The exhibition has also taught me about my development. In earlier work I made objects and hoped the idea would arrive. Here I began with a question and used each experiment to test it, and I think the show is clearer because of that. I am also more aware of the audience. Reading the cards changed my view of what viewers need: I assumed that the context would come across through the objects, but a short text on the wall about the cleared settlement might have made the projection land. I now think that there is a balance between giving too much and too little, and I had leaned too far toward silence.

For my next project I intend to continue working with absence, but to test with a viewer earlier, using a small group before the opening and not after. I also want to try the work in a place that is not a gallery, perhaps outside near a construction site, to see whether the meaning changes. Overall I judge the exhibition as successful in its physical effect on viewers and in its use of space, partly successful in its use of the projection and the repair, and valuable because the feedback gave me specific changes to make.

task: Reflect on and evaluate your exhibition and your development as an artist.
text:
Reflection on my exhibition

My exhibition was in the school gallery in March. It had four paintings of the city of Pune at night and a small sketchbook on a table. The paintings were acrylic on canvas. I put them in a row on one wall with small labels under them. The sketchbook showed my experiments.

I think the exhibition went well. A lot of people came on the opening day, including my parents and some friends and teachers. I was happy with how it looked. I think the paintings looked good together because they all had dark blue and yellow in them, so they looked like a series. My favourite painting was the bus stop at night because the yellow light looks good against the blue. I think that painting is the best one and the one that is closest to what I wanted, which was to show the city feeling lonely and empty. People who looked at it said it looked quiet, which is the mood I was trying to get.

Not everything went well. The painting of the bridge is not as good as the others. The perspective is not right and the bridge looks like it is leaning. I knew this was a problem when I was painting it, and I tried to fix it, but I ran out of time. The road in the empty street painting is still too dark. In my process work I had said that I would use lighter blue-grey for the road. I did use some but not enough, so in the exhibition you can't see the road very well and one visitor asked me what that part was. I should have tested the colour on a small canvas first.

I got some feedback from my teacher and some of my classmates. My teacher said that the paintings were very consistent but that they all looked similar and I could have tried one painting in a different time of day, to show the city in a different way. I think this is a good point, because in my research I looked at Hockney, who uses bright colours, and then I did not use any of that in the final series. Maybe I could have used it for one of the paintings. A classmate said that the labels were too small. I agree and I would make them bigger next time.

I have learned quite a lot from this project. I learned how to mix dark colours without making them muddy, and I think my brush work got better. I also learned that you have to plan an exhibition, like where to hang the paintings and how high, because I put one a bit low and people had to bend. I think my skills have developed since the start of the year, because my first painting of the bus stop was a lot more flat and now the lights look more real.

For next time I want to practise perspective and try to be braver with colour. I would also like to try a bigger canvas and maybe show a different city or a different time of day. I think I would also ask people for feedback earlier, not just at the end, so I can change things.

In conclusion, my exhibition was quite successful because the paintings look like a series and show a lonely city, but there were some problems with perspective and with the road, and I could have been more adventurous.
